results.title: Advancing CubeSat Reliability: A Model-Based Systems Engineering Approach for Fault-Tolerant, Real-Time Software
results.abstract: The University of Würzburg Experimental Satellite 5 (UWE-5) mission is advancing model-based systems engineering methodologies through the development of a modular, real-time capable on-board software framework. Designed for operation within a lightweight 128KB memory footprint, this framework integrates formalized system modeling, fault-tolerant architectures, and dynamic resource management, enabling CubeSat missions to autonomously maintain critical functions under under strict power and computational constraints. Rather than relying solely on failure recovery, the system employs proactive fault prevention to enhance mission reliability.\\ To ensure robustness, the software framework follows a digital engineering approach, incorporating modeling and simulation for early-stage validation. By leveraging FreeRTOS as a deterministic execution model, it enforces predictable task scheduling while a structured task hierarchy and adaptive task state management optimize real-time execution. These features align with modern system engineering (SE) modeling techniques, allowing for systematic performance analysis across multiple operational scenarios.\\ The framework undergoes rigorous validation and verification using a combination of hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) and software-in-the-loop (SIL) simulations, digital twin analysis, and subsystem-level testing. Initial tests confirm that hardware load limitations effectively prevent instability, while upcoming power consumption evaluations will assess the system’s ability to dynamically adapt energy usage. These validation steps represent a transition from ad hoc CubeSat software engineering to a structured, model-driven approach, ensuring improved reliability and scalability for future missions.\\ By integrating model-based verification, simulation-driven validation, and structured fault management, this work contributes to next-generation SE modeling practices that enhance mission resilience and reduce risks and costs. The structured approach moves beyond reactive software development, incorporating proactive fault detection, dynamic resource allocation, and modular task management to ensure robust execution even in resource-constrained environments. The lessons learned from this development provide valuable insights into scalable software architectures for CubeSat missions, demonstrating how a well-structured SE modeling approach can improve system reliability, maintainability, and performance.\\ This framework as part of the UWE-5 mission serves as a proof of concept for integrating SE modeling techniques into small satellite software engineering, laying the groundwork for future advancements in digital system design.

results.title: An Advanced Simulation Framework for Sail-Driven Spacecraft Dynamics and Control
results.abstract: The development of spacecrafts with solar and drag sails has gained significant interest in recent years due to their potential for fuel-free propulsion and extended mission lifetimes. This paper begins with a study of current space missions that utilize sail-driven technology, highlighting their applications, challenges, and technological advancements. Based on this analysis, we emphasize the necessity of an accurate and efficient simulation environment for testing and validating control systems designed for solar and drag sail spacecraft, particularly in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), where atmospheric drag plays a crucial role in the disturbance forces. To address this need, we present the implementation of the Drag Deorbit Device (D3) in a CubeSat platform, a propellant-less deployable and controllable drag sail system. Additionally, we propose an advanced Software-in-the-Loop (SIL) simulation framework that overcomes the limitations of previous simulation tools. The presented approach integrates Isaac Sim and Robot Operating System (ROS), leveraging the advantages of physics-based real-time simulation, high-fidelity rendering, and seamless hardware integration. In addition, enhanced GPU-accelerated physics for precise force and torque modeling, modular extensibility for integrating custom spacecraft dynamics, and real-time visualization for intuitive debugging and system analysis is considered. The presented simulation system incorporates orbital perturbations such as gravity gradient effects, atmospheric drag, gravitational anomalies, and forces from relative motion in an elliptical orbit, providing a more realistic operational environment. Instead of relying on predefined mass distribution, this approach applies drag forces directly on the spacecraft’s surface, leveraging the physics engine to naturally resolve the resulting dynamics while maintaining accuracy and enabling seamless adaptation to different spacecraft designs. The proposed SIL architecture follows a digital twin paradigm, ensuring a high-fidelity representation of the spacecraft’s dynamics and control systems within the virtual environment. This digital twin enables rapid prototyping, real-time testing, and iterative refinement of control strategies before deployment in space. By bridging the gap between simulation and real-world implementation, the presented system significantly enhances the reliability and robustness of solar sail spacecraft operations. Through this work, we demonstrate the reliability and accuracy of the proposed system using real data, validating its effectiveness for spacecraft simulation and control in LEO. Additionally, we analyze deorbiting maneuvers to assess the system’s performance in end-of-mission scenarios.

results.title: Validation of Alba CubeSat’s Thermal Model: from simulations to experimental testing
results.abstract: Thermal modelling is a critical aspect of spacecraft design, ensuring components operate within safe temperature limits in the harsh environment of space. This paper presents a case study on the validation of the thermal model for the student project Alba CubeSat from the University of Padova. AlbaSat is a 2U CubeSat entirely developed by student which participated in the Fly Your Satellite! Design Booster programme in 2024 and was supported by ESA during the development of its satellite design. The team has now been selected for the ESA Fly Your Satellite! Test Opportunity programme which ensures the chance to conduct thermal tests at ESA’s facilities “ESEC-Galaxia” in Belgium allowing the students to test the CubeSat’s thermal performance in a thermal vacuum chamber (TVAC). This opportunity enables the comparison of results with those from thermal analyses and the validation the thermal model through the creation of a digital twin. The paper provides a detailed description of the Structural-Thermal Model (STM) developed by the students to ensure an accurate representation of the CubeSat’s thermal behaviour. It outlines the setup and methodology of the thermal analyses conducted using the Radian Systems software, highlighting the specific configurations and assumptions made during the simulations. The mathematical results will be compared with the data collected by the thermocouples during thermal balance procedure to understand which assumptions worked and which parameters could be further improved to obtain even more reliable results A key aspect of this research is its educational value. The entire process, from analysis to testing and validation, is carried out by students, offering hands-on experience in spacecraft thermal application.

results.title: Architecture of a Simulation Test Bench for Operating Large Satellite Constellations
results.abstract: The approach of using FlatSats to aid the development and testing of a mission has been adopted effectively for CubeSats and small satellites. However, when considering a satellite constellation, the FlatSat approach can become limited, which is where simulating the interaction between the space and ground segments of large constellations offers a powerful enhancement. Moreover, such a simulation can be employed to evaluate new technologies and quantify their potential impact in the operation of a constellation. This paper presents an innovative architecture for a simulator designed to precisely meet these challenges.\\ The simulator deploys the NASA Operational Simulator for Small Satellites (NOS3), building on its heritage, open source components, active development and support. The use of NOS3 as the underlying simulation engine ensures compatibility with a wide range of hardware and software systems, which facilitates the testing and validation of satellite designs. It also allows for the incorporation of additional data sources and the emulation of hardware components, thereby contributing to the realism of the simulation.\\ Our proposed architecture addresses the challenges of simulating large satellite constellations, including scaling, computational efficiency and fidelity of the system modelling. A key feature of the simulator is its modularity, which allows for the integration of different flight software frameworks, subsystem models and ground segment software. These, in combination, permit different types of constellations to be simulated.\\ The simulator uses a fully containerized and microservice architecture, which ensures its portability and ease of deployment across different computing environments. This also facilitates the management of dependencies, isolation and rapid scaling of the simulation environment. Furthermore, the simulator can be run on a self-hosted infrastructure, providing users with full control over their simulation environment and data. This is particularly beneficial for organizations with strict data security requirements or those wishing to integrate the simulator into their existing infrastructure. Alternatively, the architecture can be easily deployed in a cloud-based infrastructure. The details of the design, its implementation, and its performance in several simulation scenarios will be presented.\\ We will also present how this architecture can be deployed as an operational simulator or as a test bench for new technologies, such as exploring the use of a Digital Twin in the operation of a satellite constellation.

results.title: Perception data system for satellite monitoring of strategic assets
results.abstract: Considering the different ways of applying nanosatellites, their inherent cost advantages, and the fact that this field represents a strategic area, the development of the Perception system for data collection via satellite is proposed. The Perception is a system for monitoring and producing strategic assets that uses the CubeSat standard as an instrument for the transition from scientific research to the product of technological innovation for sustainable development. Specifically, we aim to create a concept of operation, bringing the digital twin approach to deliver, among others, a new small satellite simulation environment based on the hardware-in-the-loop concept integrating the STK software, Helmholtz cage, air bearing top tables, and a flat satellite with an SDR payload for store-and-forward applications. The expected outcomes include a structured engineering model to define and validate the architecture of complex systems based on the CubeSat standard. The pilot project is aimed at collecting data via satellite from the K34 Tower of the Large-Scale Biosphere-Atmosphere Program in the Amazon (LBA), whose data is used to monitor carbon flow, among other applications. The K34 Tower is in the Amazon rainforest, approximately 64km from Manaus city, Brazil. Applications aimed at tracking unmanned aerial vehicles that support environmental monitoring activities will also be considered. Moreover, the restructuring of the entire Laboratory of Simulation and Control of Aerospace Systems, LODESTAR, at the University of Brasília is being guided by the concepts and methods of the Perception system, seeking to innovatively integrate the digital twin concept into its new physical and logical architecture. This work presents an overview of the Perception data system, its main architectures and systems, and future contributions.

results.title: Spacecraft digital engineering: the tale of “digital twins” and lessons learned
results.abstract: Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach has proved its efficiency in the design of many complex systems. It provides a mechanism for sequential linking of requirements, logical elements, and simulation models, while all information is stored in the central “the only source of truth” database. In this study, we looked at the status of existing simulation models in spacecraft engineering domain and means of connecting them into a “digital twin”. We evaluated the complexity of modelling required to analyze an astrophysical mission based on a constellation of CubeSats. The main mission goal is to demonstrate coordinated observation of gamma ray events. Conceptual design of satellites can be successfully performed based on 1D modelling, with some interfaces to detailed 3D analysis. For example, ValiSpace offers an excellent product for 1D modelling and offers a wide range of interfaces. We set out to put together the best tools available (including PLMs) on the market for detailed 3D design. The approach has been validated while building two 3U CubeSats launched in August 2022. We investigated the classical domains of a space project: mission design, systems engineering, environment modelling, mechanical and thermal design, electrical systems, communication systems, payload simulation, electronics development, flight software, attitude determination and control system and electric propulsion. A “Digital Twin” can be defined as a physics-based description of the system resulting from the generation, management, and application of data, models, and information from authoritative sources across the system’s lifecycle. The Digital Engineering approach should have a virtual product description and a virtual process definition, as well as continuous connections and physics-based simulation. Despite a clear and concise definition, this concept is hard to implement. Here we tried to analyze why. We have analyzed in detail all domains that were mentioned above to understand what tools are used there and how we can connect them to each other. We will discuss the main difficulties encountered (model complexity, interfaces, amount of work required and last-minute changes) to establish a “digital twin”. Our conclusion is that the key activity all teams must go through is to optimize how much resource will be devoted to documentation and modelling vs. how many people will be involved in assembly, integration, and testing activities.

results.title: Hardware-in-the-loop simulation framework for CubeSats proximity operations: application to the Milani mission
results.abstract: Milani is a 6U CubeSat that will be released by Hera in proximity of the Didymos binary asteroid. Milani will demonstrate autonomous GNC capability for CubeSats in deep space enhancing the scientific outcome of the mission. The Deep-space Astrodynamics Research and Technology (DART) Group at Politecnico di Milano is responsible for the Milani Mission Analysis, GNC and Image Processing (IP) design. Operations in proximity of minor bodies demand high levels of autonomy to achieve cost effective, safe, and reliable solutions. The On-Board Software has a central role in these applications, thus it must be extensively tested and validated to satisfy mission requirements and to guarantee robustness to uncertainties. A robust and standardized methodology to design, validate, and test vision-based AOCS algorithms is fundamental to achieve fast prototyping while facing at the same time limited availability of resources and time. This paper presents a modular and flexible approach, developed by DART Group, used to validate Milani’s GNC algorithms with camera-and processor-in-the-loop simulations. This framework is characterized by three elements: 1) a functional engineering simulator for six-degrees-of-freedom closed-loop simulations, 2) a vision-based navigation test-bench for camera-in-the-loop simulations, and 3) a single-board computer to test the algorithm in a representative environment of the on-board computer. The first element is the modular CuBesat ORbit and Gnc (CUBORG) tool, developed in MATLAB/Simulink at DART Lab. This contains a high-fidelity model of the environment suitable for simulating different operative scenarios, and a digital twin of the spacecraft AOCS. The modularity adopted during the implementation allows to easily switch from one configuration set, in terms of sensors, actuators and AOCS software modules, to another, with minimum effort. Camera-in-the loop simulations are performed with the in-house developed Tiny Versatile 3D Reality Simulation Environment (TinyV3RSE). It is composed of a high-resolution screen which displays synthetic images as seen from the probe during the mission, and stimulates, through a collimator, the camera mounted in the facility. The third element is a Raspberry Pi which is selected as external board to run processor-in-the-loop simulations. The proposed approach shows testing and validation for the Milani GNC and IP, assessing consistency and robustness against real hardware limitations. These results also represent a step forward in proving the feasibility of on-board implementation, thus enabling autonomous GNC capability for CubeSat platforms in deep-space missions.

results.title: STRATHcube: A CubeSat Against Space Debris
results.abstract: The responsible management of space debris is critical for the continued use of space. The STRATHcube project purposes a CubeSat which focusses on two issues of space debris - detection and removal. There is an increasing need to detect, track and catalogue debris in the Low Earth Orbit (LEO). One method to do so is by using Passive Bistatic Radar (PBR). The project purposes to launch the CubeSat into LEO as a PBR technology demonstrator, where a signal processor algorithm developed at the University of Strathclyde to detect debris will be tested. The concept involves a radar receiver and a patch antenna on-board the CubeSat from which the CubeSat will be able to detect radio signals from the operating satellites orbiting in a higher orbit. If debris were to pass between the CubeSat and the transmitting satellite, this signal would be disturbed, indicating the presence of debris. If successful, the technology demonstration will provide an alternative to conventional ground-based tracking that is cheaper and more available to the space community. Furthermore, once adopted in industry, this method can be upscaled to provide data at increased accuracy. As a secondary payload, the STRATHcube project aims to provide data on fragmentation of solar panels upon re-entry into the atmosphere. To reduce the volume of debris in low orbits, the Design for Demise (D4D) initiative champions removal of debris via uncontrolled atmospheric re-entry in which satellites completely demise. Current D4D analysis tools under-predict the effectiveness of break up upon re-entry due to a lack of re-entry data – in particular fragmentation data. The STRATHcube project, with its secondary payload, aims to provide data on the fragmentation of solar panels during re-entry by utilising thermal imaging cameras, mechanical break switches and thermal sensors. This will allow for the gathering of data regarding the conditions experienced during re-entry into the atmosphere. With this flight data, STRATHcube aims to provide greater validation and verification of satellite re-entry modelling tools that currently exist, as well as providing the framework for future fragmentation studies. To verify the life cycle of the CubeSat, an Integrated Systems Tool (IST) has been developed. Using MATLAB code, the IST creates a digital twin of the CubeSat which provides a high-fidelity simulation of the propagation as well as interlinking subsystems of STRATHcube (AOCS, power, thermal, mission analysis). The IST will verify the component and orbit selection prior to launch of the STRATHcube mission.
